newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania presidential vote a judgement of the past.
newsitem.headline: Romania presidential vote a judgement of the past.

text.p: Romanians who voted former communists out of government must choose in a weekend presidential poll between an incumbent in power since 1989 and a challenger urging them to complete the break with the past.

President Ion Iliescu, who came to power in the aftermath of the 1989 execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, held a four-point edge in the first round over Emil Constantinescu. He tells voters he can offer a counterweight to a government and legislature now controlled by his centrist rivals.

Constantinescu, a bearded academic, says a vote for him will pass judgment not only on the mass poverty he blames on Iliescu's seven years in office but on five decades of Communist rule that preceded it.

"Governments come and go but you only elect a president every four years," Iliescu's campaign video tells voters. "The president gives you assurances for tomorrow and helps you through rainy days. Why change for the sake of change?"

Constantinescu hits home on plunging living standards and wages reduced to about one-third of those in the other ex-Communist states to which Romanians like to compare themselves -- Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.
"How can you sleep at night knowing about all these problems?" he asked Iliescu during a television debate.
"This is not about politics. I've been through villages and seen the children and their desperate mothers. Don't go telling me measures are being taken and improvements being made."
Constantinescu says he wants to get on with pledges his Democratic Convention (CDR) made to cut taxes, increase social benefits and reinvigorate the economy within 200 days.

The CDR will form the backbone of the new government, along with Roman's Social Democrats, after routing Iliescu's leftist party in parliamentary elections this month and throwing it out of government for the first time since 1989.
Constantinescu received backing in the run-off from former Prime Minister Petre Roman, who was third in the opening round.
The sole opinion poll published between the two rounds gives Constantinescu a 53-47 edge over the current president.
That poll was taken before this week's television debates, in which newspapers say Constantinescu outscored the president. Surveys are in any case generally unreliable in Romania.
Campaigning, due to close at midnight on Thursday, has grown increasingly bitter.
An aggressive television campaign by Iliescu warns farmers and tenants that Constantinescu is intent on restoring pre-war landowners liable to take back their homes and workplaces.
It suggests he would threaten national unity by granting autonomy to 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians. Constantinescu denies the allegations and enraged Hungarians say they will vote for him to a man.
The historical evolution of the post-Communist period has also come under close scrutiny.
Constantinescu reflects the disappointment of liberals who say the 1989 upheaval was a coup to keep Communists in power.
He also accuses Iliescu of encouraging miners who later smashed their way through central Bucharest to denounce opposition parties and reforms. Iliescu denies the allegations.
The independent daily Adevarul said the campaign boiled down to two radically different visions of the presidency.

"Will President Constantinescu with a new government and parliament fulfil his seductive programme?" it said in an editorial. "Will president Iliescu facing a hostile parliament offer a chance to a programme he does not believe in? Each has a very different notion about what it means to be president."
